newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan PM unveils plans to take more powers.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan PM unveils plans to take more powers.

text.p: New Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, in an apparent political coup, unveiled plans on Monday to amend the constitution, curtail the powers of the president and let "the light of democracy" shine on Pakistan.

He said in a televised broadcast his Pakistan Muslim League Party and its allies had decided to repeal parts of the constitution's controversial Eighth Amendment, which empowers the president to sack a prime minister, dissolve parliament and appoint armed forces chiefs.
The amendment, a relic from the military rule by the late General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq, has been used to sack four prime ministers in eight years.
Sharif, whose party and allies have the two-thirds parliamentary majority required to rewrite the constitution, did not specify the exact parts he wanted to change.
But he said: "The controversial portions of the Eighth Amendment will go away with their bitter memories and the dear homeland will glitter with the light of democracy."

He said his plan had the approval of President Farooq Leghari, who used his Eighth Amendment powers in November to sack Benazir Bhutto as prime minister on disputed charges of corruption and misrule and dissolve the National Assembly (lower house of parliament).

Sharif, whose Muslim League won a landslide victory in the February 3 elections, said he met Leghari at the president's home village in Punjab province on Monday and "he willingly agreed to this decision".
"This is the first time in Pakistan's history that a serious and sensitive constitutional problem has been resolved in the spirit of understanding and co-operation," he said.
Sharif had been expected to use his speech only to explain a package of economic reforms and tax cuts announced last week.

But political sources said deputies of the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) and their allies urged Sharif at a meeting in Islamabad on Monday to scrap the amendment, which they said was hampering democratic institutions.

Zia, who introduced the Eighth Amendment as part of a bargain to end martial law, used it to sack his own hand-picked prime minister Mohammad Khan Junejo in May 1988 before being killed in a mysterious plane crash in August.
Then Bhutto was sacked first by then president Ishaq Khan in 1990 and then by Leghari last November. Sharif was sacked by Ishaq Khan in 1993.
Sharif said in his speech that after his landslide "mandate for a change" in the February 3 elections he could not be a silent spectator to all the ills that Pakistan was suffering from.

"Therefore, the PML and its allied parties decided after serious and prolonged consultations to restore the supremacy of parliament, to restore people's power back into their hands and restore the democratic system to the shape left by the father of the nation, Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah.
"We have decided to repeal those parts of the Eight Amendment which have been clouding the democratic horizon."

Bhutto has accused Leghari and a caretaker government he appointed after sacking her of rigging the February 3 elections to deal a crushing defeat to her Pakistan People's Party. But she says will be back Sharif in repealing the Eighth Amendment.
